I went after the lineation, because a verifier who has just moved the start of a quotation is a verifier who has been inside the poem's line breaks, and that is exactly where a plausible-looking reconstruction gets made. It held, word for word and break for break.

WHAT I READ. I downloaded the PDF the evidence names, eclass.uoa.gr ENL605 ‘Marianne Moore - Nevertheless.pdf’, and extracted it with pdftotext -layout this run, so I have the whole poem in front of me rather than a snippet. It runs in tercets from ‘you've seen a strawberry / that's had a struggle; yet / was, where the fragments met,’ through the prickley-pear and the grape tendril, and it ends:

  The weak overcomes its
  menace, the strong over-
  comes itself. What is there

  like fortitude! What sap
  went through that little thread
  to make the cherry red!

So every claim in the note is true. The closing tercet does open with ‘like fortitude!’; ‘What sap’ does end that line; ‘What is there’ is the last line of the tercet before; and the four lines quoted are the last four lines of the poem. The card's line breaks are the poem's, in that order, and the lowercase line heads ‘like’, ‘went’ and ‘to’ are kept as Moore prints them, which is what rule 7 asks for when it says the poem's own capitals at the line head. The verifier's correction was the right one and it fixed a real fault: starting at ‘like fortitude!’ would have begun the card mid line and mid sentence, whereas starting at ‘What is there’ gives a complete exclamation, ‘What is there like fortitude!’, and then the question about the sap.

THE ONE STRUCTURAL THING I WOULD FLAG, WHICH IS NOT ENOUGH TO REFUTE. There is a stanza break between ‘What is there’ and ‘like fortitude!’, and the card renders it with the same ‘ / ’ it uses for the line breaks inside the tercet. Rule 7 defines only ‘ / ’ and says nothing about stanza divisions, so the card breaks no rule, but a reader is shown four lines of one stanza where the poem has one line and then a tercet. The alternatives are worse: quoting the final tercet alone starts mid sentence, and quoting six lines drags in ‘menace, the strong over- / comes itself’ with Moore's hyphen splitting a word across lines, which would be unreadable on a card. The verifier chose correctly. If the editor wants the structure visible, the note could add one clause saying the poem's stanzas are tercets and the first line quoted closes the preceding one. That is a note improvement, not a citation fault.

EVERYTHING ELSE PASSES. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], marianne moore at 0 of 3, not banned, and she is a woman, which the month's floor of eight wants. Attribution is not in dispute and nothing on the misattribution list touches Moore. No speaker is owed: this is the poet in her own voice, not a character. The book is right, and it is a fact worth keeping straight, that the collection and its title poem share a name: Nevertheless (New York: Macmillan, 1944) is the slim wartime volume that also carries ‘In Distrust of Merits’ and ‘A Carriage from Sweden’, and ‘Nevertheless’ is the title poem in it. The note says so, which is why the doubled title in the source line does not read as an error. Scope: verse, 1944, well before 1999, not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory. Publishable: a strawberry, a cherry, a grape tendril and a prickly pear; there is no wound in it anywhere. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. The source line leads with the author's name, carries no em dash and no straight quote, ends the quotation in an exclamation mark, and runs 99 characters. Theme fit is the best in this batch: ‘What is there like fortitude!’ is Courage in Trial stated outright, and the poem earns it through eleven tercets of roots growing in frozen ground rather than asserting it.

The only soft spot left is that my witness is a transcription rather than the Macmillan sheets, and I say so plainly. But it is a transcription of the whole poem, not an extract, its line breaks and hyphenations are Moore's throughout (‘star- / fish’, ‘over- / comes’, ‘some- / times’), which is not what a quotation site produces, and the four lines under test contain no dash, no hyphen split and no ambiguous mark, so there is nothing in them for a transcription to have got wrong. Ships as written.
